newsitem.title: ITALY: World Food Summit will pledge to slash hunger.
newsitem.headline: World Food Summit will pledge to slash hunger.

text.p: An unprecedented food summit next week will commit world leaders to an effort to reduce the number of people who go hungry from 840 million to half that figure by the year 2015, organisers said on Tuesday.

The pledge is the most specific undertaking made in an agreed declaration and plan of action drawn up for the World Food Summit, which the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) will hold in Rome from November 13 to 17.

Senior FAO officials hailed agreement in advance on the two texts as a first for a major international conference and a breakthrough that would allow heads of state and government to focus instead on how to make the words reality.

They also rejected the view that compromise language avoiding contested references to "the right to food for all" and a pledge to end hunger within one generation -- as well as lack of hard cash -- would transform the summit into an empty event.
"This is the first time world leaders will come together to address the crucial problem of hunger," Kay Killingsworth, the summit secretary-general, told a news conference.
"What has come out of the negotiating process is what we think are very concrete and practical agreements."
She said the summit would focus public opinion on "the most basic and crucial issue facing humanity and that is ensuring ...food security for everyone".
FAO, which is based in Rome, has invited 196 heads of state and government to the gathering, which will be opened with a message delivered by Pope John Paul.
The U.N. agency has refused so far to identify the participants, citing security reasons, though Killingsworth said on Tuesday that 100 leaders had confirmed they would attend.
Diplomats say Cuban President Fidel Castro is likely to be among them and that he could use the occasion as a chance for an historic meeting with the Pope.

U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali will also address next Wednesday's opening session, at which the Declaration on World Food Security and a seven-point Plan of Action are scheduled to be adopted.

Wording of the two texts was finally agreed by national delegates at a four-day meeting in Rome last week after six months of haggling, thus avoiding the bickering which has dominated several past major U.N. conferences.
"The fact that this document is already agreed...is a first in international conferences," Killingsworth said. "What it allows is for the leaders to come and focus on the future."

The summit declaration reaffirms "the right of everyone to have access to safe and nutritious food, consistent with the right to adequate food and the fundamental right of everyone to be free from hunger".

Wording in previous drafts about the "right to food for all" was excised from the final version, reflecting concern by some rich countries including the United States that it could lead to lawsuits demanding aid or special trade provisions.

"We pledge our political will and our common and national commitment to achieving food security for all and to an on-going effort to eradicate hunger in all countries, with an immediate view to reducing the number of undernourished people to half their present level no later than 2015," the declaration says.
A senior FAO official, Jacques Vercueil, said countries wanted to make a pledge they believed they could keep.

He noted that the last major gathering on hunger, the 1974 World Food Conference, had aimed to eradicate undernourishment within a decade. More than 20 years on the number has fallen by only 80 million despite substantial growth in food supplies.

Current FAO estimates are that 840 million people, or 20 percent of the world's population, are undernourished, and that the figure will drop to 680 million, or 12 percent, by 2010 unless determined action is taken to lower it further.
